claim: Within vertebrates, examples of losses include flight in birds, armor plates in sticklebacks, and the ability to synthesize vitamin C in bats.
source: Within vertebrates, examples of losses include flight in birds, armor plates in sticklebacks, and the ability to synthesize vitamin C in bats (Burga et al., 2017; Cui et al., 2011; Le Rouzic et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies.

claim: Many instances of trait loss occur in parallel across multiple independent lineages.
source: Strikingly, many instances of trait loss occur in parallel across multiple independent lineages (e.g. Colosimo et al., 2004, Drouin et al., 2011, and Harshman et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Most mammals possess three visual opsins: rhodopsin (RHO) in rods, and opsin one long-wave sensitive (OPN1LW) found in L-cones, and opsin one short-wave sensitive (OPN1SW) found in S-cones.
source: Most mammals possess three visual opsins: rhodopsin (RHO) in rods, and opsin one long-wave sensitive (OPN1LW) found in L-cones, and opsin one short-wave sensitive (OPN1SW) found in S-cones.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about mammalian vision.

claim: There have been >20 independent losses of cone-opsins in mammals, with associated reduction in color sensitivity.
source: Reconstructions of the highly complex evolutionary history of mammalian vision suggest that there have been >20 independent losses of cone-opsins, with associated reduction in color sensitivity (e.g. Bowmaker, 1998, Emerling et al., 2015, Lucas et al., 2003, Porter et al., 2012 and Yokoyama et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Some cetacean and xenarthran lineages appear to have lost both of their cone-opsins.
source: This is exemplified in some cetacean and xenarthran lineages, which appear to have lost both of their cone-opsins (Emerling and Springer, 2015; Meredith et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Evolutionary reconstructions of color vision have nearly all been based solely on opsin gene sequences, with gene expression and protein data limited or missing for most mammalian species.
source: Evolutionary reconstructions of color vision have nearly all been based solely on opsin gene sequences, with gene expression and protein data limited or missing for most mammalian species, including cetaceans and primates (but see Kraus et al., 2014, Peichl et al., 2017, Schweikert et al., 2016 and Wikler and Rakic, 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations indicating exceptions to the general pattern.

claim: No large-scale comparative study of color vision in mammals has considered each of the steps in protein production (e.g., transcription, translation).
source: To date, no large-scale comparative study of color vision in mammals has considered each of the steps in protein production (e.g., transcription, translation).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the authors' review of the literature.

claim: Noctilionoid bats underwent ecological diversification approximately 40 million years ago.
source: These bats underwent ecological diversification approximately 40 million years ago (Rojas et al., 2012; Rossoni et al., 2017), and show marked morphological and sensory adaptations linked to their unparalleled dietary specializations (Davies et al., 2013; Dumont et al., 2012; Hayden et al., 2014; Monteiro and Nogueira, 2010; Yohe et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Noctilionoid bats show marked morphological and sensory adaptations linked to their unparalleled dietary specializations.
source: These bats underwent ecological diversification approximately 40 million years ago (Rojas et al., 2012; Rossoni et al., 2017), and show marked morphological and sensory adaptations linked to their unparalleled dietary specializations (Davies et al., 2013; Dumont et al., 2012; Hayden et al., 2014; Monteiro and Nogueira, 2010; Yohe et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Until recently it was thought that S-opsin, encoded by the OPN1SW gene, was likely functional across the suborder Yangochiroptera.
source: Until recently it was thought that S-opsin, encoded by the OPN1SW gene, was likely functional across the suborder Yangochiroptera (e.g. Butz et al., 2015, Feller et al., 2009, Marcos Gorresen et al., 2015, Gutierrez et al., 2018, Müller et al., 2009, Winter et al., 2003 and Zhao et al., 2009a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Multiple independent lineages with diverse ecologies show evidence of OPN1SW pseudogenization.
source: However, with increased taxonomic sampling of neotropical bat species this has been shown to not be the case, and multiple independent lineages with diverse ecologies (e.g. blood feeding, plant-visiting species) show evidence of OPN1SW pseudogenization (Kries et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent published studies.

claim: Lineages shown to have lost their S-opsins are from the Noctilionoidea superfamily.
source: Notably, lineages shown to have lost their S-opsins – and thus by association UV-sensitivity – are from the Noctilionoidea superfamily.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the cited literature.

claim: Within the Yinpterochiroptera, multiple losses of S-opsin function have been documented in lineages of Old World fruit bats as well as horseshoe bats and Old World leaf-nosed bats that have evolved a derived form of laryngeal echolocation.
source: In contrast, within the other bat suborder – the Yinpterochiroptera – multiple losses of S-opsin function have previously been documented in lineages of Old World fruit bats as well as horseshoe bats and Old World leaf-nosed bats that have evolved a derived form of laryngeal echolocation (Zhao et al., 2009a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Bat short-wave opsins are sensitive to UV based on inferences from amino acid sequence analyses and action spectra.
source: The loss of S-opsins could have profound impacts on bat visual acuity, as inferences from amino acid sequence analyses and action spectra suggest that bat short-wave opsins are sensitive to UV, and their retention is possibly related to the demands of visual processing in mesopic, or low-light, conditions (Zhao et al., 2009a), and/or plant visiting (Butz et al., 2015; Feller et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2008; Müller et al., 2009; Müller et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: OPN1SW was only detected in just over half of the species assayed (n = 32).
source: Surprisingly, OPN1SW was only detected in just over half of the species assayed (n = 32), including all members of the primarily frugivorous subfamily Stenodermatinae, which invariably retain their S-cones (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: All members of the primarily frugivorous subfamily Stenodermatinae invariably retain their S-cones.
source: Surprisingly, OPN1SW was only detected in just over half of the species assayed (n = 32), including all members of the primarily frugivorous subfamily Stenodermatinae, which invariably retain their S-cones (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: OPN1SW was found to be absent in approximately one third of species assayed (n = 18), including representative species from five bat families.
source: In contrast, OPN1SW was found to be absent in approximately one third of species assayed (n = 18), including representative species from five bat families.
evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: This study provides the first evidence of S-opsin loss in non-noctilionoid Yangochiroptera (Chilonatalus micropus, Eptesicus fuscus and Molossus molossus).
source: Thus, we not only find evidence of widespread loss of S-opsins within the noctilionoids but also find the first evidence of S-opsin loss in non-noctilionoid Yangochiroptera (Chilonatalus micropus, Eptesicus fuscus and Molossus molossus).
evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Almost all cones expressed either OPN1SW or OPN1LW protein, with no strong evidence of co-localization of both proteins.
source: Consistent with cone-specific roles, we found that almost all cones expressed either OPN1SW or OPN1LW protein, with no strong evidence of co-localization of both proteins (Figure 2 and Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: Evidence of at least partial OPN1SW mRNA transcripts was found in a total of 34 bat species.
source: We found evidence of at least partial OPN1SW mRNA transcripts in a total of 34 bat species; thus, expression was only absent in five of the species assayed.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: OPN1SW expression was absent in five species: Chilonatalus micropus, Mormoops blainvillei, Macrotus waterhousii, Brachyphylla (nana) pumila and Lionycteris spurrelli.
source: Absences of OPN1SW transcripts were phylogenetically widespread, and included divergent species from three families (Natalidae: Chilonatalus micropus; Mormoopidae: Mormoops blainvillei and Phyllostomidae: Macrotus waterhousii, Brachyphylla (nana) pumila and Lionycteris spurrelli) (see Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: The complete RHO and OPN1LW transcript was recovered from all taxa assessed (n = 39).
source: In comparison, we were able to recover the complete RHO and OPN1LW transcript from all taxa assessed (n = 39; Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: A total of nine lineages were found to possess OPN1SW transcripts but lack OPN1SW protein.
source: Comparison of our OPN1SW transcript and protein data revealed numerous conflicts in species-specific absences, with a total of nine lineages found to possess OPN1SW transcripts but lack OPN1SW protein (see Figures 1, 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of RNA-Seq and immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: Nine species possess OPN1SW transcripts but lack OPN1SW protein: Molossus molossus, Pteronotus parnellii, Desmodus rotundus, Trachops cirrhosus, Tonatia saurophila, Gardnerycteris crenulatum, Monophyllus redmani, Erophylla bombifrons, and Carollia brevicauda.
source: These species included Molossus molossus, Pteronotus parnellii, Desmodus rotundus, Trachops cirrhosus, Tonatia saurophila, Gardnerycteris crenulatum, Monophyllus redmani, Erophylla bombifrons, and Carollia brevicauda.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of RNA-Seq and immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The partial D. rotundus fragment (~300 base-pairs of exons 2–4) contained a premature stop codon.
source: The partial D. rotundus fragment (~300 base-pairs of exons 2–4) contained a premature stop codon – confirmed by PCR and the recently published common vampire bat genome.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data confirmed by PCR and genome data.

claim: For E. bombifrons, the longest of three OPN1SW transcripts contained a putative four base-pair deletion and retained a portion of the intron between exons 2 and 3.
source: We recovered a total of three OPN1SW transcripts for E. bombifrons from our transcriptome assembly, and the longest of these transcripts contained a putative four base-pair deletion and retained a portion of the intron between exons 2 and 3.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: D. rotundus and E. bombifrons appear to have transcribed OPN1SW pseudogenes.
source: Therefore, D. rotundus and E. bombifrons appear to have transcribed OPN1SW pseudogenes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the RNA-Seq data showing disrupted sequences.

claim: For C. brevicauda and T. saurophila, RNA-Seq assemblies recovered a single and complete OPN1SW mRNA transcript containing all five exons and the 3' UTR.
source: First, for two species, C. brevicauda and T. saurophila, our RNA-Seq assemblies recovered a single and complete OPN1SW mRNA transcript containing all five exons and the 3' UTR, albeit with ~5 codons missing at the 5' end in one of these taxa (C. brevicauda).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In P. parnellii (n = 4), 2, 4, 5, or 18 variants were assembled per individual, and no intact mRNA isoforms were recovered among these variants.
source: Finally, for Pteronotus parnellii (n = 4), we detected the most splice variation, with 2, 4, 5, or 18 variants assembled per individual. Furthermore, in P. parnellii, we were unable to recover any intact mRNA isoforms among these variants.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In P. parnellii, an entirely missing exon five and partial deletion of exon 1 was seen in two individuals.
source: Many of the variants were repeated across individuals; for example, an entirely missing exon five (despite the presence of the up-/down-stream sequences), and partial deletion of exon 1, was seen in two individuals (see Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: An in-frame three base-pair deletion (Y190del) was detected in three of four P. parnellii individuals sequenced.
source: We also detected an in-frame three base-pair deletion (Y190del) in three of four P. parnellii individuals sequenced.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ORF recovered by manual PCR of exons 3–4 was intact in C. micropus and B. (nana) pumila.
source: Among the four species lacking the OPN1SW transcript and protein, we found the ORF recovered by manual PCR of exons 3–4 was intact in C. micropus (the single sampled Natalidae species), as well as the unrelated phyllostomid B. (nana) pumila.
evidence: The claim is based on PCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The genomic sequences recovered by blastn was disrupted by insertions and deletions resulting in premature stop codons in Mormoops blainvillei, Macrotus waterhousii, and Lionycteris spurrelli.
source: In contrast, the genomic sequences recovered by blastn was disrupted by a number of insertions and deletions resulting in premature stop codons in Mormoops blainvillei, Macrotus waterhousii, and Lionycteris spurrelli.
evidence: The claim is based on genomic sequence data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In Phyllonycteris poeyi, data from four individuals showed S-cone presence, yet the transcript of one other individual was inferred to be non-functional based on a four base-pair insertion.
source: The exception was Phyllonycteris poeyi, for which data from four individuals showed S-cone presence, yet the transcript of one other individual was inferred to be non-functional based on a four base-pair insertion (confirmed via PCR).
evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemistry and RNA-Seq data confirmed by PCR.

claim: Within the OPN1SW sequences of most species examined, the ATG start codon was found to be three codons downstream relative to that of the human orthologue.
source: We also note that within the OPN1SW sequences of most species examined, the ATG start codon was found to be three codons downstream relative to that of the human orthologue (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence alignment data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: Complete correlation was found between the presence of the transcript and protein for OPN1LW.
source: In contrast to the mismatches between OPN1SW mRNA and OPN1SW protein, we found complete correlation between the presence of the transcript and protein for OPN1LW in these species.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of RNA-Seq and immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A significantly higher ω was found in lineages with a pseudogenized OPN1SW in both the OPN1SW gene (ωbackground = 0.13; ωOPN1SW.intact=0.24; ωOPN1SW.pseudo=0.78; χ2(2)=70.99, p=3.84e-16) and the OPN1LW gene (ωbackground = 0.08; ωOPN1SW1.intact=0.08; ωOPN1SW.pseudo=0.19; χ2(2)=9.18, p=0.01).
source: We found a significantly higher ω in lineages with a pseudogenized OPN1SW in both the OPN1SW gene (ωbackground = 0.13; ωOPN1SW.intact=0.24; ωOPN1SW.pseudo=0.78; χ2(2)=70.99, p=3.84e-16), and the OPN1LW gene (ωbackground = 0.08; ωOPN1SW1.intact=0.08; ωOPN1SW.pseudo=0.19; χ2(2)=9.18, p=0.01).
evidence: The claim is based on molecular evolution analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: No differences in ω were found across the different lineages for RHO, indicating strong and negative selection in this gene.
source: In contrast, we found no differences in ω across the different lineages for RHO, indicating strong and negative selection in this gene (Table S2 in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on molecular evolution analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Background branches (non-frugivorous) had a significant and slightly higher ω for RHO (ωbackground = 0.04; ωfugivory= 0.01; χ2(1)=13.77, p=2.07e-4).
source: We found no differences in rates for OPN1SW or OPN1LW, however background branches (non-frugivorous) had a significant and slightly higher ω for RHO (ωbackground = 0.04; ωfugivory= 0.01; χ2(1)=13.77, p=2.07e-4; Table S3 in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on molecular evolution analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mean cone densities ranged from 2500 to 7500 cones/mm2 for L-cones, and 327 to 5747 cones/mm2 for S-cones.
source: We found photoreceptor density varied among examined species (Figure 2, Table S4 in Supplementary file 2), with mean cone densities ranging from 2500 to 7500 cones/mm2 for L-cones, and 327 to 5747 cones/mm2 for S-cones (Figure 2, Table S4 in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on photoreceptor quantification data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: In every case, the density of S-cones was lower than that of L-cones.
source: In every case, the density of S-cones was lower than that of L-cones.
evidence: The claim is based on photoreceptor quantification data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Densities of both cone types tended to be highest near the center of the retina in all species.
source: Densities of both cone types tended to be highest near the center of the retina in all species.
evidence: The claim is based on photoreceptor quantification data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Bat species with S-cones had significantly higher densities of L-cones, with the presence of S-cones increasing the ln-transformed density of L-cones by 43%, explaining on average ~24% of the variance in density between species.
source: Bat species with S-cones had significantly higher densities of L-cones, with the presence of S-cones increasing the ln-transformed density of L-cones by 43%, explaining on average ~24% of the variance in density between species (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on Bayesian regression analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Frugivory was the best factor for explaining the presence of S-cones.
source: Comparisons of the coefficients, which are all at the same scale because they are multipliers of the presence of a particular ecology, showed frugivory was the best factor for explaining the presence of S-cones (Figure 5, Tables S5-S7 in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on Bayesian regression analyses presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: The predominance of fruit in the diet increases the odds of having S-cones roughly 39 times, and explains about 50% of the between-species variance in the presence of the S-cone.
source: The predominance of fruit in the diet increases the odds of having S-cones roughly 39 times, and explains about 50% of the between-species variance in the presence of the S-cone (Table S7 in Supplementary file 2, Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is based on Bayesian regression analyses presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: In P. quadridens, three of 17 individuals were found to lack S-cones.
source: In Pteronotus quadridens, three of 17 individuals were found to lack S-cones.
evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: This study documents molecular signatures consistent with as many as 17 instances of parallel loss in S-opsins.
source: Across our study taxa, we documented molecular signatures consistent with as many as 17 instances of parallel loss in S-opsins, and equated these with a minimum of three putative routes leading to the failure of the formation of the S-opsin cones (Figures 1, 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is based on the combined data from DNA, RNA, and protein analyses presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: Three putative routes lead to the failure of the formation of the S-opsin cones: pseudogenization, intact gene sequence that did not result in mRNA transcript, and intact OPN1SW transcripts that did not result in the corresponding S-cone protein.
source: First, we found evidence of multiple independent instances of pseudogenization, associated with either absent or fragmentary mRNA transcripts. Second, we found evidence of an apparently intact gene sequence that did not result in a mRNA transcript. Finally, we recovered putatively intact OPN1SW transcripts that did not result in the corresponding S-cone protein, which in some species appears to arise from aberrant isoforms.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined data from DNA, RNA, and protein analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mismatches between opsin coding DNA and mRNA have not previously been documented in mammals, including bats.
source: To our knowledge such mismatches between opsin coding DNA and mRNA have not previously been documented in mammals, including bats, although this largely reflects a shortage of suitable datasets.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the authors' review of the literature.

claim: The OPN1SW mRNA of the blind mole-rat Spalax ehrenbergi has been found to contain introns.
source: Indeed it is particularly noteworthy that the OPN1SW mRNA of the blind mole-rat Spalax ehrenbergi has also been found to contain introns (David-Gray et al., 2002; Esquiva et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Diet appears to be the primary selective agent for maintaining S-opsin function.
source: Diet therefore appears to be the primary selective agent for maintaining S-opsin function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Bayesian regression analyses showing frugivory as the best explanatory factor.

claim: Some predominantly nectarivorous species from both independent nectar-feeding lineages have lost their S-cones, while others have retained them (e.g. Anoura geoffroyi).
source: We also found that while some predominantly nectarivorous species from both independent nectar-feeding lineages, have lost their S-cones, others have retained them (e.g. Anoura geoffroyi).
evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Behavioral assays have been used to infer that some nectarivorous phyllostomid species appear to be color blind, and thus may be able to utilize UV reflectance to locate flowers via an alternative rod-based mechanism.
source: While the loss of S-opsins in flower visiting bats may seem maladaptive, behavioral assays have previously been used to infer that some nectarivorous phyllostomid species appear to be color blind, and thus may be able to utilize UV reflectance to locate flowers via an alternative rod-based mechanism (Winter et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The main difference in molecular selection was between species with an OPN1SW ORF and a pseudogene at this locus.
source: As expected once pseudogenization has occurred, the main difference in molecular selection was between species with an OPN1SW ORF and a pseudogene at this locus.
evidence: The claim is based on molecular evolution analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Protein composition should more closely reflect visual ecology than high rates of sequence evolution and pseudogenization in the relevant opsin.
source: Therefore, protein composition should more closely reflect visual ecology than high rates of sequence evolution and pseudogenization in the relevant opsin, as the latter only responds to long-term functional loss.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the analyses showing stronger ecological associations with protein presence than with ORF status.

claim: The strongest ecological association was with the presence of S-cones (rather than with earlier steps in protein production).
source: We further tested this inference by modeling the presence of an OPN1SW ORF, mRNA, or protein as a function of ecological covariates, finding the strongest ecological association—estimated by higher coefficients—with the presence of S-cones (rather than with earlier steps in protein production).
evidence: The claim is based on Bayesian regression analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The discovery of loss of gene function in non-HDC Mormoopidae (e.g. Mormoops blainvillei and Pteronotus davyi) calls into question the sensory trade-off hypothesis within this family.
source: Furthermore, the discovery of loss of gene function in non-HDC Mormoopidae, e.g. Mormoops blainvillei and Pteronotus davyi, also call into question the sensory trade-off hypothesis within this family.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing S-opsin loss in species without high-duty cycle echolocation.

claim: The utility of long-term fixed specimens for immunohistochemical staining of proteins (e.g. vimentin and GFAP) has been described previously.
source: Despite this, the utility of long-term fixed specimens for immunohistochemical staining of proteins (e.g. vimentin and GFAP) has been described previously (Hühns et al., 2015; Thewissen et al., 2006), including visual opsins in some museum specimens (~20 years old and using the same S-opsin antibody as used in the current study) (Nießner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Good IHC staining for both S- and L-cones was recovered from the oldest sampled museum specimen with a confident date, an Artibeus fraterculus collected in 1921.
source: In line with this, we were able to recover good IHC staining for both S- and L-cones from our oldest sampled museum specimen with a confident date, an Artibeus fraterculus collected in 1921 (see Figure supplement S3).
evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: S-opsin assays were inconclusive for six species (T. brasiliensis, P. hastatus, S. tildae, S. ludovici, P. dorsalis and C. villosum) represented by museum samples due to low signal-to-background ratios, but L-opsin assays were successful in these species.
source: We note, however, that our S-opsin assays were inconclusive for six species (T. brasiliensis, P. hastatus, S. tildae, S. ludovici, P. dorsalis and C. villosum) represented by museum samples due to low signal-to-background ratios, but L-opsin assays were successful in these species.
evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: L-cones are present at higher densities than S-cones.
source: Because L-cones are present at higher densities than S-cones (this study and Müller et al., 2009), we were able to more readily detect L-cones even in more poorly preserved retina.
evidence: The claim is based on photoreceptor quantification data from this study and a cited study.

claim: Fresh specimen of M. molossus from Belize and two older museum specimens from 1968 from Uruguay all lacked S-cones, whereas a published record of an individual from an unknown geographical locality showed S-cone presence.
source: In another instance, our fresh specimen of M. molossus from Belize and two older museum specimens from 1968 from Uruguay all lacked S-cones, whereas a published record of an individual from an unknown geographical locality showed S-cone presence (Nießner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemistry data from this study compared to a published record.

claim: Low gene expression can limit the number of representative reads in RNA-Seq datasets for transcript assembly.
source: For example, low gene expression can limit the number of representative reads in RNA-Seq datasets for transcript assembly (e.g. Zhao et al., 2011) and this caveat likely applies to shortwave-sensitive opsins that show low S-cone densities, inferred loss of function in some taxa, and also low expression levels based preliminary expression analyses (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and preliminary data from this study.

claim: For Monophyllus redmani, Trachops cirrhosus and Pteronotus parnellii, assembled transcripts matched published assembled mRNA contigs, PCR amplicons and genomic sequences, respectively.
source: For example, for Monophyllus redmani, Trachops cirrhosus and Pteronotus parnellii we were able to confirm that our assembled transcripts matched published assembled mRNA contigs, PCR amplicons and genomic sequences, respectively (Gutierrez et al., 2018; Tsagkogeorga et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of RNA-Seq data from this study with published data.

claim: For Mormoops blainvillei and Macrotus waterhousii, the absence of OPN1SW mRNA transcripts and S-cones was supported by disrupted ORFs in published genome datasets.
source: For Mormoops blainvillei and Macrotus waterhousii, the absence of OPN1SW mRNA transcripts and S-cones was supported by disrupted ORFs in published genome datasets, as well as the highly divergent and fragmented transcripts recovered by a recent study, which our visual inspections suggest may be due to cross contamination or misassembly (Gutierrez et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of data from this study with published genome data.

claim: The retention of introns in OPN1SW mRNA as well as the expression of pseudogenized opsin mRNA are both supported by earlier studies.
source: The observed retention of introns in OPN1SW mRNA as well as the expression of pseudogenized opsin mRNA are both supported by earlier studies (David-Gray et al., 2002; Schweikert et al., 2016); however, alternative scenarios for these findings could include gDNA contamination, sequencing of immature mRNA or low-level cross contamination resulting in the assembly of highly divergent transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies, but also acknowledges alternative explanations.

claim: There is no clear relationship between RIN score or sequencing depth and presence of OPN1SW mRNA.
source: However, the lack of a clear relationship between RIN score or sequencing depth and presence of OPN1SW mRNA (data not shown), together with the presence of the two other visual opsins in all samples, suggests this should be sufficient.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis from this study.

claim: The presence of the two other visual opsins (RHO and OPN1LW) in all samples suggests that one individual per species should be sufficient for mRNA evidence.
source: However, the lack of a clear relationship between RIN score or sequencing depth and presence of OPN1SW mRNA (data not shown), together with the presence of the two other visual opsins in all samples, suggests this should be sufficient.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing consistent recovery of RHO and OPN1LW.

claim: Findings of mismatches between genotype and phenotype indicate a role for transcriptional and even translational control in the process of opsin loss.
source: Although variation in the complement of photoreceptors across vertebrates is usually explained by disruptions to the protein-coding sequence (e.g. Mundy et al., 2016 and Zhao et al., 2009a), findings of mismatches between genotype and phenotype also indicate a role for transcriptional and even translational control in this process.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing mismatches between DNA, RNA, and protein.

claim: Because routes of gene loss are mainly studied at the genetic level or, in fewer cases, at the transcriptomic level, the input of changes in translation and other connections between the genetic, transcriptomic, and proteomic levels may be being underestimated.
source: It follows that because routes of gene loss are mainly studied at the genetic level or, in fewer cases, at the transcriptomic level, the input of changes in translation and other connections between the genetic, transcriptomic, and proteomic levels may be being underestimated.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings of this study and the state of the field.

claim: Current studies both underestimate the extent of parallel losses, and might lead to an incomplete picture based on genes alone.
source: Hence, current studies both underestimate the extent of parallel losses, and might lead to an incomplete picture based on genes alone.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings showing multiple routes to opsin loss beyond pseudogenization.

claim: Assessments of visual perception based purely on genotypic analyses of either opsin sequences or RNA transcripts can be misleading.
source: In conclusion, our findings reveal that assessments of visual perception based purely on genotypic analyses of either opsin sequences or RNA transcripts can be misleading, and may even obscure the evolutionary processes and ecological agents of selection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings showing mismatches between DNA, RNA, and protein.

claim: Findings indicate a role for transcriptional and even translational control in the process of opsin loss.
source: Although variation in the complement of photoreceptors across vertebrates is usually explained by disruptions to the protein-coding sequence (e.g. Mundy et al., 2016 and Zhao et al., 2009a), findings of mismatches between genotype and phenotype also indicate a role for transcriptional and even translational control in this process.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing mismatches between DNA, RNA, and protein.

claim: Apparent shifts in translation and transcription precede pseudogenizing changes in ORFs.
source: More broadly, our results highlight the importance of rapid trait loss in evolution, with apparent shifts in translation and transcription that precede pseudogenizing changes in ORFs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing protein and transcript loss in species with intact ORFs.

claim: Eye transcriptomes were generated for 46 individuals (39 species) including biological replicates of Pteronotus parnellii (n = 4), Artibeus jamaicensis (n = 4) and Phyllops falcatus (n = 2).
source: Eye transcriptomes were generated for 46 individuals (39 species) including biological replicates of Pteronotus parnellii (n = 4), Artibeus jamaicensis (n = 4) and Phyllops falcatus (n = 2).
evidence: This is a description of the methods and sample sizes used in the study.

claim: Immunohistochemistry was performed on at least three retinas from two individuals for each species.
source: For each species, IHC was performed on at least three retinas from two individuals (for details see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: Eye tissue was obtained from 59 New World bat species, of which 49 were collected from the wild and 34 from the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH), with 24 species common to both sources.
source: We obtained eye tissue from 59 New World bat species, of which 49 were collected from the wild and 34 from the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH), with 24 species common to both sources (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the sample collection for the study.
